questions.question: You have 3 red stars. You get 4 more stars. How many stars do you have now?
questions.explain: Put 3 and 4 together to make 7. A common trap is counting the 3 as your first count, which gives 6, one too few.

questions.question: There are 5 ducks in the pond. 3 more ducks come. How many ducks are in the pond now?
questions.explain: Put 5 and 3 together to get 8. If you count the 5 as your first count, you stop at 7, one too few.

questions.question: You have 6 crayons. Your friend gives you 3 more. How many crayons do you have together?
questions.explain: Put 6 and 3 together to get 9. Counting the 6 as your first count gives 8, which is one too few.

questions.question: 4 fish swim to the tank. 5 more fish swim to the same tank. How many fish are in the tank?
questions.explain: Put 4 and 5 together to get 9. Taking 5 away from 4 gives 1, but the story is about adding groups together.

questions.question: Sam has 7 cookies. Mom bakes 4 more. How many cookies does Sam have now?
questions.explain: Put 7 and 4 together to get 11. If you count the 7 as your first count, you stop at 10, one too few.

questions.question: Lily picks 6 flowers. Her sister picks 5 flowers. They put them all in one vase. How many flowers are in the vase?
questions.explain: Put 6 and 5 together to get 11. Counting the 6 as your first count gives 10, one too few.

questions.question: You have 9 stickers. You win 2 more at a game. How many stickers do you have together?
questions.explain: Put 9 and 2 together to get 11. Taking 2 away from 9 gives 7, but here we are adding, not taking away.

questions.question: There are 8 chairs at the table. Dad puts 4 more at the table. How many chairs are at the table now?
questions.explain: Put 8 and 4 together to get 12. If you count the 8 as your first count, you stop at 11, one too few.

questions.question: You have some fish in a jar. You put 5 more fish in. Now there are 9 fish. How many fish were there before?
questions.explain: If adding 5 makes 9, the starting group was 4, because 4 and 5 together make 9. Adding 9 and 5 gives 14, but we need the starting number.

questions.question: You have 4 marbles. You get 3 more. Then a friend gives you 2 more. How many marbles do you have?
questions.explain: Add 4 and 3 to get 7, then put 2 more to get 9. A common mistake is subtracting the last group or forgetting it.

questions.question: Which one means putting 5 and 4 together?
questions.explain: Putting together means joining two groups into one bigger group. Taking away means subtracting, which is the opposite idea.

questions.question: You, your sister, and your brother put your stickers in one book. You have 5, she has 4, and he has 3. How many stickers are in the book?
questions.explain: Put all three groups together: 5 plus 4 is 9, and 9 plus 3 is 12. A common trap is counting the starting number as your first count, which gives one too few.

questions.question: You put 5 fish in a tank. Your friend puts some more in, and now there are 12. How many did your friend put in?
questions.explain: Put 5 and the unknown together to make 12. Counting on from 5: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 — that is 7 fish. Do not add 5 and 12 together to get 17.

questions.question: Maya has 7 gummy bears. Her friend gives her 6 more, and Maya says she has 13. Is Maya right?
questions.explain: Maya is right — putting 7 and 6 together gives 13. The most common mistake is counting the 7 as your first count, which makes the answer 12.

questions.question: You put 6 apples in a basket, and your mom puts 4 more in. Your dad adds some more, and now there are 15. How many did your dad put in?
questions.explain: First put 6 and 4 together to make 10. Then find what goes with 10 to make 15 — that is 5. Do not subtract when the story is about adding more.
